Pickleball in the sky: A new Berkeley club plays 6 stories above downtown

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:14
Instaread
Since May, members have been swatting pickleballs on three courts atop a parking garage. The club’s courts are open to non-members twice a week.
by Nathan Dalton Aug. 10, 2026, 7:00 a.m.Aug. 7, 2026, 2:35 p.m.

Share this:

A local entrepreneur has built a little slice of pickleball heaven on top of a six-story parking garage in downtown Berkeley. 

Neighborhood Pickleball, which opened in May, was founded by Jim Jenkins, a software engineer and pickleball fanatic who lives in Orinda. He was inspired to open the space after visiting Urban Pickleball Club, a members-only pickleball oasis located on top of a parking garage in Austin, Texas. 

While getting in some games at the club, Jenkins spent a lot of time speaking with its owner, who encouraged him to open his own parking garage-topped club back in California. Jenkins kind of laughed off the suggestion at first, but couldn’t get the idea out of his head. And a few months after his visit began searching for suitable parking garages across the Bay Area. He finally found what he called a “dream location” on top of a parking structure on Allston Way next door to the Downtown YMCA.

Amy Murray, the chef and owner of Revival Bar & Kitchen, plays a fair amount of pickleball at the Y, and recently got a chance to play at Neighborhood Pickleball. She was blown away. 

“It’s an incredible setting,” she said. “There were red-tailed hawks flying above us and really beautiful views to the hills and to the Bay and to Oakland. So you get an incredible perspective, which is neat. And then they’re just state-of-the-art courts.”

Like many other pickleball enthusiasts, Jenkins caught the pickleball bug during the pandemic, and was soon playing in tournaments across the West Coast. He’s visited so many facilities that he knows what separates a good court from a bad one, and for Neighborhood Pickleball he wanted the best. 

“One thing that was very important to me was to have a space that high-level or pro pickleball players in the Bay Area would want to come to,” he said. 

That meant not just “pro-grade” court surfaces, but making sure the courts were placed in a way that the sun wouldn’t be an issue. He placed fencing along the perimeter and put up screens to keep the Bay-fueled winds down. 

But, inspired by Urban Pickleball in Austin, Jenkins also wanted to make sure to optimize for the social and community aspects of the game

“Most pickleball facilities optimize for sheer court numbers and don’t necessarily do a great job at community,” said Jenkins.

But Urban Pickleball felt different. “It was the first time I’d been to a private club that really just felt like a neighborhood park,” he said. 

To inspire that same feeling, Jenkins added 1,500 square feet of astroturf, along with picnic tables and adirondack chairs. He’s also keeping the membership numbers low. He currently has a waiting list close to 200 people, but he’s going to cap membership at 75 people total, which is low for a club with three courts.

“If you go to any public park on a Saturday you can play one game every 45 minutes,” said Jenkins. “And so what I really want to offer is an experience where the members feel like these are their own courts.” 

Memberships cost $99 per month after a $199 initiation fee. Members can bring unlimited guests for $15 per guest per day. The self-service courts are open daily from 8 a.m.-8 p.m., and are reserved though an app that Jenkins built himself. Members can access the courts using the parking garage’s elevators or stairs and then let themselves in using a Bluetooth lock.

Jenkins also offers public access to the courts every Tuesday and Thursday from 5:30-7:30 p.m. for $15 per person.

“It’s kind of what you would find at any neighborhood park, where you can just show up any time in that window and try to get some games in,” he said. 

Getting people to the club so far has not been an issue. He’s actually running into the opposite problem. 

“I can’t get people to leave,” he said. “They come and play, and then they go downstairs and grab food, and then they bring food back up, and everybody just hangs out.”

Neighborhood Pickleball, 2061 Allston Way, 6th Floor, Berkeley. Hours: Daily 8 a.m.-8 p.m. for members. Connect via Instagram.
